title: Al-Bassama
intro: Ibn Abdun, vizier and secretary to the Aftasid kings of Badajoz, wrote this elegy when the Almoravids killed the last of them, al-Mutawakkil Umar, with his sons al-Fadl and al-Abbas; al-Marrakushi dates their deaths to the start of 485 AH (1092 CE). It opens with a warning against time and its treachery, then names one after another the kings, peoples and heroes time has destroyed, from Dara and the Persian emperors and the lost tribes of Arabia to the Prophet's Companions and the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs. Only after the caliphs' titles does it turn to the sons of al-Muzaffar, and it ends in praise of itself. Known as al-Bassama, it was given a long historical commentary by the Andalusian man of letters Ibn Badrun of Silves, which tells the story behind every name, and al-Marrakushi wrote that in it Ibn Abdun took “a path no one had taken before him”.

translation: Time strikes at the trace after the thing itself;
so why weep over shapes and likenesses?
1.sharh: Time takes a thing and then takes even the trace it leaves, so nothing of the departed survives. Weeping over bodies and images is pointless, since the mourner will soon follow them.

translation: I warn you, I warn you, sparing no counsel,
against sleeping between the lion's fang and claw.
2.sharh: He repeats the warning with all the care he can give: to trust the world is to sleep between a lion's teeth and claws. A note in Ibn Badrun's commentary reads it as a warning against making peace with the days, which are an enemy.

translation: Time is at war, though it may show a face of peace;
its white days and black nights are white swords and brown spears.
3.sharh: Time only pretends to make peace. Its days and nights are its weapons: the white days are white blades, the black nights brown spears. Spear shafts were cane, so “brown” stands for spears, and “white” serves for both days and swords.

translation: There is no truce between the head held fast
by the swordsman's hand and the keen blade of hard steel.
4.sharh: A sword shows no mercy to the head it falls on, and time shows none to people; its blows never pause. The Arabic calls the blade “male”, said of a sword forged from the hardest iron.

translation: Do not be fooled by your world when it seems to sleep:
its eyes know no trade but staying awake.
5.sharh: The world only seems to sleep: its eyes are always open, watching for a chance to strike at whoever trusts its calm. The real sleeper is the one it fools, like the man of the line before who dozes between the lion's fang and claw.

translation: What is it with the nights? May God lift our stumble
at their hands, and may the hand of change betray them.
6.sharh: He breaks off in wonder at what the nights do, and prays twice in passing: that God set people back on their feet after the nights trip them, and that the nights be struck in turn by the changes they deal out.

translation: At every moment, in every limb,
they leave wounds on us, though the eye cannot see them.
7.sharh: The nights are always wounding people, even when the wounds do not show; they wear a man down little by little without his noticing. Limb and wound share a root in Arabic.

translation: They please you with a thing only to beguile you,
like a snake that springs from the flowers at whoever picks them.
8.sharh: The world's pleasures are bait. The danger hides in what delights, like a snake among flowers that strikes the moment a hand reaches for them.

translation: How many states have the nights served with victory,
then left nothing of them. Ask your memory for word of them.
9.sharh: The nights serve a dynasty with victories for a while, then wipe it out. With this line the poem begins its long roll of fallen kings and peoples, from ancient Persia to Baghdad.

translation: They brought Dara down, and blunted the edge of his killer,
who had been a keen sword against kings, its steel shining.
10.sharh: Dara, the last of the ancient Persian kings, fell to Alexander, and then the nights dulled Alexander too, though he had cut through kings like a fine sword. Killer and killed end alike.

translation: They took back from the sons of Sasan what they had given,
and left the sons of Greece no trace.
11.sharh: Kingship is a loan the nights call in when they please: the Sasanian emperors of Persia lost all they had been given, and the Greeks vanished without a mark.

translation: They made Tasm's sister follow it, and there came back
on Ad and Jurhum what unpicks the strongest rope.
12.sharh: Tasm and Jadis, sister tribes of ancient Arabia, perished one after the other, and the same undoing fell on Ad and Jurhum. The Arabic plays on ada, “came back”, and Ad, the tribe.

translation: They spared none of the men of state of Yemen,
and sheltered none of the men of high goals of Mudar.
13.sharh: Neither the old kings of southern Arabia nor the great men of the northern Arabs escaped. Ibn Badrun notes that the poet names no one here, gathering them all under the two names.

translation: They scattered Saba' to every far corner,
and none leaving at nightfall met one leaving at dawn.
14.sharh: The people of Saba' were dispersed so widely that they never came together again. The line echoes the Quran on them: “We scattered them utterly” (34:19).

translation: They carried out their sentence on Kulayb, and cast
Muhalhil out between the earth's hearing and its sight.
15.sharh: Kulayb, whose pride was a byword, was murdered, and his brother Muhalhil, after years of vengeance, met his own death alone, where no one saw or heard. Neither glory nor revenge saved either of them.

translation: They did not give the Wandering King his health back,
nor turn Asad away from their lord, Hujr.
16.sharh: Imru' al-Qays, the great poet of pre-Islamic Arabia, died far from home of a poison that ate his body, and his father Hujr was killed by the tribe of Asad over whom he ruled.

translation: They wore down the clan of Dhubyan and their brothers,
Abs, and bit the sons of Badr by the water.
17.sharh: Time humbled the brother tribes of Dhubyan and Abs through forty years of war over a horse race, and caught the sons of Badr, the chiefs of Dhubyan, at a pool, where Abs took its revenge on them.

translation: They sent after Adi, in Iraq, by the hand
of his own son, the man with red eyes and red hair.
18.sharh: Al-Nu'man, the red-haired king of al-Hira in Iraq, had killed the poet Adi ibn Zayd. Adi's son then turned the Persian emperor against al-Nu'man, who was put to death, so the killer followed his victim.

translation: They destroyed Abarwiz through his son, and flung
Yazdajird to Merv, and he never came back.
19.sharh: Khusraw Parviz was overthrown and killed by his own son, and Yazdajird, the last Persian emperor, fled before the Arab armies as far as Merv, where he was killed.

translation: They carried Yazdajird as far as China, and cut away from him
all but the Persians: the hosts of the Turks and the Khazars.
20.sharh: Time drove Yazdajird to the edge of the known world, as far as China, and stripped away the foreign allies he had gathered, so that only his own Persians stood by him at the end.

translation: The keen swords of Rustam and the spears
of Dhu al-Hajib did not keep Sa'd from him in that disaster.
21.sharh: At al-Qadisiyya the Persian commander Rustam and the standard-bearer Dhu al-Hajib could not stop Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and the Persian empire fell. “Daughter of changes” is an Arabic name for a catastrophe.

translation: The sons of Badr perished on the day of the well,
and the well of Badr hurried those in it to Hell.
22.sharh: Two wells and two Badrs: the well where the sons of Badr met their end, probably the pool of line 17, and the well at the battle of Badr, into which the Prophet's enemies from Quraysh were thrown. From their well the pagan dead of Badr go on to Hell.

translation: They tore Ja'far apart with swords, and snatched
Hamza from his thicket, Hamza who slaughtered camels for his guests.
23.sharh: Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin, was cut to pieces at Mu'ta, and Hamza, his uncle, called the Lion of God, was killed at Uhud. “Wronging the camels”, the Arabic phrase, was praise for a host who slaughtered them freely.

translation: They raised Khubayb high on a tall beam,
and pressed Talha the bountiful into the dust.
24.sharh: Khubayb, a Companion captured by the Meccans, was crucified outside Mecca, and Talha, famous for his generosity, fell at the Battle of the Camel.

translation: They dyed Uthman's white hair with blood, strode on
to al-Zubayr, and felt no shame before Umar.
25.sharh: Three of the foremost Companions were murdered: the caliph Uthman in his own house, al-Zubayr after he had left the Battle of the Camel, and the caliph Umar, stabbed at prayer. Not even Umar's awesome presence held the nights back.

translation: They had no regard for Abu al-Yaqzan's companionship,
and gave him no provision but thin milk in a little cup.
26.sharh: Ammar ibn Yasir, one of the first Muslims, fought for Ali at Siffin. Thirsty in battle, he was handed watered milk and said the Prophet had told him milk would be his last drink; he was killed that day.

translation: They gave Abu Hasan as prey to the most wretched one's sword,
and put Husayn into the hands of Shimr.
27.sharh: Ali, the fourth caliph, was struck down by the Kharijite Ibn Muljam, whom the Prophet had foretold as the most wretched of men, and Ali's son al-Husayn was killed at Karbala by Shimr.

translation: If only, when they ransomed Amr with Kharija,
they had ransomed Ali with whomever they pleased.
28.sharh: Three Kharijites swore to kill Ali, Mu'awiya and Amr ibn al-As on the same night. Amr was ill and sent Kharija to lead the prayer in his place, and Kharija was killed instead. Ali had no such stand-in.

translation: They destroyed Ibn Ziyad for al-Husayn, yet he was not worth
a sandal strap of his that had fallen, or a fingernail.
29.sharh: Ubaydallah ibn Ziyad, the governor who sent the army to Karbala, was killed in his turn, but his blood could not pay for al-Husayn's. Ibn Badrun traces the phrase to Muhalhil, who told a man he killed for Kulayb, “Be the price of Kulayb's sandal strap.”

translation: They turbaned the temples of Abu Anas with the edges of swords,
and the spears of Zufar did not turn death from him.
30.sharh: Al-Dahhak, who declared for Ibn al-Zubayr in Syria, was cut down at Marj Rahit, and the spears of his ally Zufar, a famous horseman, could not save him. The swords wound round his head make him a turban of death.

translation: They brought Mus'ab down from the top of a towering height
in which al-Mukhtar's life had once been sheltered.
31.sharh: Mus'ab took Kufa from al-Mukhtar and killed him, then lost it, and his life, to the Umayyad Abd al-Malik. The towering height, says Ibn Badrun, is Kufa itself: its many fighting men made it a fortress for each of them in turn, had they not betrayed both.

translation: They paid no heed to Ibn al-Zubayr's standing,
nor respected his refuge in the House and the Stone.
32.sharh: Ibn al-Zubayr trusted the sanctity of the Kaaba to protect him, but al-Hajjaj besieged Mecca, bombarded it with catapults and killed him. Not even God's House was a refuge from time.

translation: They did not leave Abu al-Dhubban his deadly blade;
Amr the Slapped, whom it killed, was never avenged.
33.sharh: The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik cut down every rival, among them his kinsman Amr al-Ashdaq, whose blood went unavenged. Yet the sword that won him all this could not keep death from him; Ibn Badrun reads the line as time betraying even the shrewdest of kings.

translation: They burned Zayd's remains, after the hearts
of the Quran's verses and suras had burned for him in grief.
34.sharh: Zayd, of the Prophet's house, rose against the Umayyads and was killed; his body was crucified and later burned. The poet makes the Quran itself grieve for him, as if its verses had hearts, because he was a man devoted to it.

translation: They handed al-Walid son of Yazid to his enemies,
and left no caliphate between the cup and the lute string.
35.sharh: Al-Walid II, the caliph of wine and song, was killed by the men of his cousin Yazid. A caliphate kept between the wine cup and the lute string could not last; wine, says Ibn Badrun, cost him his kingdom.

translation: Habbaba: a pomegranate seed was destined for her,
and a red one that a waft of aloeswood let fall.
36.sharh: Death can come from the smallest thing: Habbaba, the beloved singer of the caliph Yazid II, choked on a pomegranate seed in an hour of pleasure with him, and Yazid died soon after. The red thing of the second half seems to be the seed itself; the line is not in Ibn Badrun's text, and no source consulted explains it.

translation: The blades of al-Saffah did not stay far
from the head of Marwan or his wicked followers.
37.sharh: The swords of the new Abbasid dynasty did not spare the old one: they hunted Marwan down in Egypt and killed his followers. One dynasty's ruin was the next one's founding.

translation: They made the Faithful Spirit shed tears
over blood of the Prophet's house spilt in vain at Fakhkh.
38.sharh: The poet makes Gabriel weep over the blood of the Prophet's family shed at Fakhkh, which no one avenged. Ibn Badrun objects that Gabriel's tears are told of al-Husayn of Karbala, and suspects the poet confused the two, or a copyist wrote Fakhkh for al-Taff, Karbala.

translation: They made Ja'far choke, while al-Fadl looked on
and old Yahya, on the spittle of a keen blade.
39.sharh: When Harun al-Rashid destroyed the Barmakid family, he had his vizier Ja'far beheaded and threw his brother al-Fadl and his old father Yahya into prison. To make a man choke on a sword's “spittle”, its edge, is to cut his throat.

translation: They broke the covenant sworn for al-Amin, and rose
against Ja'far through his own son and his treacherous slaves.
40.sharh: Harun al-Rashid had his sons al-Amin and al-Ma'mun swear not to betray each other, and hung the oaths in the Kaaba; they went to war and al-Amin was killed. The caliph al-Mutawakkil, whose name was Ja'far, was murdered by his Turkish guards at his son's bidding, as Ibn Badrun tells it.

translation: They kept no faith with the covenants given al-Musta'in,
nor with the strong-twisted oaths made fast for al-Mu'tazz.
41.sharh: Al-Musta'in gave up the caliphate on sworn guarantees of his safety and was killed all the same, and the oaths sworn to his successor al-Mu'tazz did not save him either. Oaths are “strong-twisted” like rope, and time unpicks them.

translation: They bound every Mu'tamid fast in their loops,
and made every Muqtadir choke on their grit.
42.sharh: The titles mean “the one who relies” and “the mighty”, and each man who bore them was bound or choked in the end. Ibn Badrun lists the caliphs and kings who held each one; the poet's own age had a Mu'tamid, the king of Seville, whom the Almoravids carried off as a prisoner.

translation: They terrified every Ma'mun and Mu'taman,
and abandoned every Mansur and Muntasir.
43.sharh: Again the names are caliphs' and kings' titles, and each is turned against its meaning: the “safe” and the “trusted” are terrified, the “aided” and the “victor” are abandoned. Ibn Badrun lists everyone in the East and in al-Andalus who bore each one.

translation: They tripped the house of Abbas, may they rise again,
on the train of a shaggy calamity that never shies in fright.
44.sharh: The Abbasids stumbled over their own Turkish guards, who came to make and murder caliphs, as Ibn Badrun explains. The proverb says a shaggy camel always bolts, but this calamity stands its ground and does not go away.

translation: Sons of al-Muzaffar: the days have always been
stages on a road, and all people are travelling through them.
45.sharh: Here the poem reaches its occasion, the fall of the Aftasid kings of Badajoz. Every day is one stage of a journey whose end is death, and the Aftasids have reached it as everyone must.

translation: A curse on your day, that day, and may no night
ever be pregnant with its like in all time to come.
46.sharh: He curses the day the Aftasids fell and prays that no night will ever carry another like it. Arabic poets speak of the night as pregnant with what the morning will bring.

translation: Who now for the thrones, who for the reins,
who for the spearheads, to guide them to the breaches?
47.sharh: With the Aftasids gone there is no one to sit on the throne, ride at the head of the cavalry or lead the spears to the frontier. The question is a lament; it expects no answer.

translation: Who now for the blades and the tall spears of al-Khatt,
the tips of whose tongues are knotted with stammering and silence?
48.sharh: Swords and spears have tongues, their edges and points, which spoke in battle. Without the Aftasids to wield them they are tongue-tied.

translation: They have collared their white blades with black deaths:
marvel at that. Nothing is left of them but memories.
49.sharh: The swords that dealt death now wear it round their necks, white steel ringed with black, and the contrast is meant to astonish. All that remains of the blades and the men who bore them is remembrance.

translation: Who now for the pen, who for the mastery,
who for the generosity, or for the power to help and harm?
50.sharh: With them died the pen and the mastery of it, generosity, and the power to reward friends and punish enemies. The Aftasids were men of letters as well as war: al-Muzaffar compiled a vast anthology, and al-Mutawakkil wrote verse and prose. The Arabic plays on yara'a, “pen”, and bara'a, “mastery”.

translation: Or for warding off catastrophe, or turning back what bears down,
or crushing a disaster that would weary fate itself?
51.sharh: The list of what is lost goes on: they were the ones who turned back disaster, even disasters too heavy for fate itself, an exaggeration of their power.

translation: Alas for generosity, alas for courage, if only they had lived,
and the grief of faith and world for Umar.
52.sharh: Umar al-Mutawakkil, the last Aftasid king, was generosity and courage in person; with him both are dead, and religion and the world alike mourn him.

translation: May a pouring cloud water the soil of al-Fadl and al-Abbas,
its bounty traced to them, and not to the rain.
53.sharh: Praying for rain on a grave is an old Arabic blessing. Here the cloud's generosity will be credited to the dead, al-Mutawakkil's sons and the king himself, because they were more generous than rain.

translation: Three of them: the two Eagles never climbed where they climbed,
nor any eagle that flies, or that does not fly.
54.sharh: The father and his two sons rose higher than the stars. “Any eagle that flies or does not fly” plays on the names of the two Eagle stars, one flying and one falling, and takes in every bird besides.

translation: Three like time's own being: since they went far from me,
time has passed on, never stopping, never turning back.
55.sharh: The three were so much the substance of his days that their going has taken time with it: since then the days run on without pause, and the good ones never return.

translation: The best of everything in it has passed,
even the pleasure of the evenings and the mornings.
56.sharh: Time has taken the best of everything with them. Since the princes died, even the simple pleasure of a cool morning or a golden evening has gone out of life.

translation: Where is the majesty whose awe lowered
our hearts, and the eyes of the shining stars?
57.sharh: Their majesty humbled people's hearts and even made the stars lower their eyes. “Where is” opens three lines of lament for the qualities that died with them.

translation: Where is the pride they set firmly
on pillars of power and of victory?
58.sharh: Their refusal to accept humiliation was a building set on pillars of power and victory, and it has fallen with them.

translation: Where is the faithfulness whose watering places they kept clear,
so that no one came down to them and found them muddied?
59.sharh: Their loyalty is pictured as a spring kept clean: anyone who came to drink from it found clear water, never mud.

translation: They were the anchoring mountains of God's earth; since they left it
it has flown apart with all on it, and found no rest.
60.sharh: The Quran speaks of mountains set firm to keep the earth from shaking. The Aftasids were those mountains for their land, and since they went it has been in upheaval.

translation: They were its lamps; since they went out, all creation,
God help us, has stumbled in a daze.
61.sharh: They were the lamps of the earth, as they were its mountains in the line before; without them all creation stumbles in the dark, and the poet cries out to God for help.

translation: They were a bone in time's throat, till its wiles lured them
with the minds of Ad, in the footsteps of al-Khidr.
62.sharh: Time could not swallow them, so it tricked them, though they had the proverbial minds of Ad, the ancient people famed for their judgment, and walked in the steps of al-Khidr, the keeper of hidden knowledge. The Arabic ahlam can also mean dreams: dreams of Ad's strength and of al-Khidr's endless life.

translation: Woe to its mother, that seeker of vengeance, taking it
from them in lions, noble men, unflinching in war.
63.sharh: Time, in whose throat the Aftasids had stuck, never lets a debt of revenge go: it took its revenge on them, and the price it exacted was lions, noble men who stood firm in battle. The poet marvels at such an avenger.

translation: Who will bring them to me, and none will, if troubles darken
and their night does not lead on to dawn?
64.sharh: He wishes for them in every kind of trouble and checks himself at once: no one can bring them back. This line and the next two open with the same words, a chant of grief.

translation: Who will bring them to me, and none will, if customs lie idle
and the tongues of tradition and history are hushed?
65.sharh: The Aftasids upheld good custom and loved history: al-Muzaffar gathered its best stories in his great anthology. Without them both fall silent.

translation: Who will bring them to me, and none will, if trials close in,
and going down to their waters holds no hope of coming back?
66.sharh: The image is from watering: going down to the water (wird) is followed by coming back from it (sadar). These trials are waters one goes down to and never leaves.

translation: To all the virtues but patience, now they are gone,
the farewell of one who waits for his reward.
67.sharh: He bids farewell to every virtue now that they are gone, except patience, which he keeps, because patience in grief earns God's reward and he means to wait for it.

translation: He hopes in “perhaps”, and has hope in its sister,
for time has many turns and many changes.
68.sharh: He clings to the words of hope, “perhaps” and its sister “it may be”. Time has many turns, and what it takes away it may in some form give back.

translation: I have hung on the ears of everyone on earth an ornament
that puts to shame the rubies and pearls on beautiful women.
69.sharh: The poet ends by praising his own poem: he has hung it on every ear like an earring, and it outshines the rubies and pearls that beautiful women wear.

translation: Travelling to the ends of the earth, cutting short
the bellowing throats that roared in desert and town.
70.sharh: A camel stallion bellows by puffing out a bladder from its mouth, the shiqshiqa, and Arabic uses the word for loud eloquence. The poem silences every orator and poet.

translation: Obeyed in its commands over minds, fulfilling
for the ears a longing never fulfilled before.
71.sharh: The poem rules its listeners' minds like a sovereign whose orders are obeyed, and gives their ears a satisfaction no other poem has given them. With this the praise of the poem, and the poem itself in the old sources, comes to an end.

translation: Then blessings on the Chosen, our master,
the Elect, the Preferred, sent forth from Mudar.
72.sharh: The poem closes with blessings on the Prophet, a descendant of Mudar. This line and the next are not in the older sources; they close the poem in the Cairo printing of Ibn Badrun's commentary.

translation: And on his family and Companions, and those who followed him,
as long as the wind blows and the clouds pour down rain.
73.sharh: The blessing extends to the Prophet's family and Companions and those who came after them, for as long as winds blow and rain falls, which is to say for ever.

1.1.4.head: العَين
1.1.4.meaning: Ayn: the thing itself, as against its trace.

2.1.4.head: أَلا
2.1.4.meaning: La aluka: I spare no effort for you.

3.2.5.head: السُّمُر
3.2.5.meaning: Sumr: “the brown ones”, spears, whose shafts were brown cane; the bid before it, “the white ones”, are swords.

4.2.4-5.head: الصّارِم الذَّكَر
4.2.4-5.meaning: “The cutting male”: a sharp sword of the hardest iron.

6.1.3-5.meaning: “May God lift our stumble”: a prayer for pardon and recovery.

7.1.7.head: جارِحَة
7.1.7.meaning: Jariha: a limb; it shares its root with jirah, wounds.

10.1.2.head: دارا
10.1.2.meaning: Dara: Darius III, the last king of ancient Persia, killed in his war with Alexander, who took his kingdom.

10.1.5.head: قاتِل
10.1.5.meaning: His killer: Alexander of Macedon, who lived only six years after Dara's death, says Ibn Badrun.

10.2.6.head: الأُثُر
10.2.6.meaning: Uthur: the rippling sheen on a fine blade.

11.1.3-4.head: بَنو ساسان
11.1.3-4.meaning: Banu Sasan: the Sasanians, the last Persian dynasty before Islam, named after Sasan, forebear of its founder Ardashir.

12.1.3.head: طَسم
12.1.3.meaning: Tasm: with its sister tribe Jadis, a lost people of al-Yamama in ancient Arabia; the two destroyed each other after Amluq, king of Tasm, wronged Jadis, as Ibn Badrun tells.

12.2.1.head: عاد
12.2.1.meaning: Ad: the people of the prophet Hud, a lost tribe destroyed by a wind, in the Quran.

12.2.2.head: جُرهُم
12.2.2.meaning: Jurhum: an ancient tribe that held Mecca and the Kaaba before it was driven out and vanished.

12.2.4-5.head: ناقِض المِرَر
12.2.4-5.meaning: “The unpicker of tight-twisted ropes”: the blow that undoes whatever is strong.

13.1.6.head: اليَمَن
13.1.6.meaning: Yemen: the southern Arabs of Qahtan, who had kings before Islam.

13.2.6.head: مُضَر
13.2.6.meaning: Mudar: ancestor of the northern Arab tribes, Quraysh among them, from whom came the Prophet and the caliphs.

14.1.2.head: سَبَأ
14.1.2.meaning: Saba': the people of Sheba in Yemen, named after their forebear; they scattered across Arabia after the dam of Ma'rib burst, as Ibn Badrun tells.

14.2.3.head: رائِح
14.2.3.meaning: Ra'ih: one who travels at evening; mubtakir, at the end of the line, one who sets out at dawn.

15.1.3.head: كُلَيب
15.1.3.meaning: Kulayb: Kulayb ibn Rabi'a, chief of Taghlib and Bakr, a byword for pride; his murder began the War of al-Basus.

15.2.1.head: مُهَلهِل
15.2.1.meaning: Muhalhil: Kulayb's brother, a poet, who avenged him for years and was killed in a lonely place, as Ibn Badrun tells.

15.2.2-5.meaning: “Between the earth's hearing and sight”: a proverb for a deserted place where no one sees or hears.

16.1.4.head: الضِّلّيل
16.1.4.meaning: Al-Dillil: “the Wandering King”, Imru' al-Qays, the pre-Islamic poet-prince; he went to the Byzantine emperor for an army to avenge his father and died at Ankara, Ibn Badrun says of a poisoned robe the emperor sent him.

16.2.3.head: أَسَد
16.2.3.meaning: Asad: the tribe of Banu Asad, who killed their king Hujr.

16.2.6.head: حُجر
16.2.6.meaning: Hujr: Hujr ibn al-Harith, Imru' al-Qays's father, king over Asad, who killed him.

17.1.3.head: ذُبيان
17.1.3.meaning: Dhubyan: brother tribe of Abs; the two fought the forty-year War of Dahis and al-Ghabra', named after the two horses in the race that began it.

17.2.1.head: عَبس
17.2.1.meaning: Abs: Dhubyan's brother tribe, the tribe of Antara.

17.2.3-4.head: بَنو بَدر
17.2.3-4.meaning: Banu Badr: chiefs of Fazara in Dhubyan; Hudhayfa and Hamal, the sons of Badr, led them.

17.2.6.head: النَّهَر
17.2.6.meaning: The water: the pool of al-Haba'a, where Abs killed Hudhayfa and Hamal, says Ibn Badrun.

18.1.2.head: عَدِيّ
18.1.2.meaning: Adi: Adi ibn Zayd, a Christian poet of al-Hira and the Persian emperor's Arabic secretary; he had al-Nu'man made king, and al-Nu'man jailed and killed him, as Ibn Badrun tells.

18.2.2.head: اِبن
18.2.2.meaning: His son: Zayd ibn Adi, who worked on the emperor until he had al-Nu'man killed.

18.2.3-5.meaning: “The red of eye and hair”: al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, king of al-Hira, whose skin was blotched; so the poet Abu Qardudah of Tayyi' described him, warning a friend against his company. The emperor Abarwiz had him killed.

19.1.2.head: أَبرَويز
19.1.2.meaning: Abarwiz: Khusraw II Parviz, one of the greatest Sasanian emperors, killed by his son Shiruya.

19.2.1.head: يَزدَجِرد
19.2.1.meaning: Yazdajird: Yazdegerd III, the last Sasanian emperor, who fled before the Muslim armies and was killed near Merv in 32 AH (652 CE).

19.2.3.head: مَرو
19.2.3.meaning: Merv: a great city of Khurasan; a millwright on the Murghab river took Yazdajird in for the night and killed him, as Ibn Badrun tells.

20.1.3.head: الصّين
20.1.3.meaning: China: Yazdajird sent his treasure there, went there himself and came back, says Ibn Badrun.

20.2.5-6.head: التُّرك وَالخَزَر
20.2.5-6.meaning: The Turks and the Khazars: peoples beyond Khurasan whose help Yazdajird sought; their khagan withdrew and left him.

21.1.4.head: رُستُم
21.1.4.meaning: Rustam: commander of the Persian army at al-Qadisiyya, killed there in 14 AH (636 CE).

21.2.1-2.head: ذو الحاجِب
21.2.1-2.meaning: Dhu al-Hajib: Khurrazad, who carried the emperor's banner at al-Qadisiyya, says Ibn Badrun.

21.2.4.head: سَعد
21.2.4.meaning: Sa'd: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, the Companion who led the Muslims at al-Qadisiyya.

22.1.3-4.head: بَنو بَدر
22.1.3-4.meaning: The sons of Badr: the chiefs of Fazara, two of whom were killed at the pool of al-Haba'a (line 17); al-Fath ibn Khaqan, introducing the poem, writes of “the two sons of Badr at the well of al-Haba'a”.

22.2.1-2.head: قَليب بَدر
22.2.1-2.meaning: The well of Badr: where the Meccan dead were thrown after the battle of Badr in 2 AH (624 CE).

22.2.6.head: سَقَر
22.2.6.meaning: Saqar: one of the Quran's names for Hell.

23.1.2.head: جَعفَر
23.1.2.meaning: Ja'far: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, Ali's brother, who lost both hands and his life at the battle of Mu'ta in 8 AH (629 CE).

23.2.2.head: غيل
23.2.2.meaning: Ghil: a lion's thicket; Hamza was called the Lion of God.

23.2.3.head: حَمزَة
23.2.3.meaning: Hamza: Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle, killed at Uhud in 3 AH (625 CE).

24.1.2.head: خُبَيب
24.1.2.meaning: Khubayb: Khubayb ibn Adi, a Companion captured in an ambush and sold in Mecca, where he was crucified at al-Tan'im, as Ibn Badrun tells.

24.2.2-3.head: طَلحَة الفَيّاض
24.2.2-3.meaning: Talha the Bountiful: Talha ibn Ubaydallah, a leading Companion famed for his generosity, killed at the Battle of the Camel in 36 AH (656 CE).

25.1.3.head: عُثمان
25.1.3.meaning: Uthman: Uthman ibn Affan, the third caliph, killed in his house in 35 AH (656 CE).

25.2.2.head: الزُّبَير
25.2.2.meaning: Al-Zubayr: al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, the Prophet's cousin and disciple; he left the Battle of the Camel and was killed by treachery in Wadi al-Siba', as Ibn Badrun tells.

25.2.6.head: عُمَر
25.2.6.meaning: Umar: Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph, stabbed at the dawn prayer in 23 AH (644 CE).

26.1.3-4.head: أَبو اليَقظان
26.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Yaqzan: Ammar ibn Yasir, an early Companion, killed at Siffin fighting for Ali.

26.2.4.head: الضَّيح
26.2.4.meaning: Dayh: thin milk mixed with water.

27.1.3.head: أَشقى
27.1.3.meaning: “The most wretched”: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, Ali's killer, so called after the Prophet's words to Ali about the most wretched man, who would dye his beard with the blood of his head.

27.1.4-5.head: أَبو حَسَن
27.1.4-5.meaning: Abu Hasan: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth caliph, killed in 40 AH (661 CE).

27.2.3.head: حُسَين
27.2.3.meaning: Husayn: al-Husayn ibn Ali, the Prophet's grandson, killed at Karbala in 61 AH (680 CE).

27.2.5.head: شَمِر
27.2.5.meaning: Shimr: Shimr ibn Dhi al-Jawshan, a commander of the army that killed al-Husayn.

28.1.4.head: عَمرو
28.1.4.meaning: Amr: Amr ibn al-As, conqueror and governor of Egypt.

28.1.5.head: خارِجَة
28.1.5.meaning: Kharija: a man of Amr's clan who led the prayer in Amr's place and was killed by the assassin, who said, “I wanted Amr, and God wanted Kharija.”

29.1.2-3.head: اِبن زِياد
29.1.2-3.meaning: Ibn Ziyad: Ubaydallah ibn Ziyad, governor of Kufa, who sent the army against al-Husayn; he was killed by Ibrahim ibn al-Ashtar, al-Mukhtar's general.

29.2.1.head: باءَ
29.2.1.meaning: Yabu': to be a fit price in blood for another man.

30.1.4-5.head: أَبو أَنَس
30.1.4-5.meaning: Abu Anas: al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Fihri, killed at Marj Rahit in 64 AH (684 CE).

30.2.6.head: زُفَر
30.2.6.meaning: Zufar: Zufar ibn al-Harith of Kilab, a renowned horseman who fled from Marj Rahit.

31.1.2.head: مُصعَب
31.1.2.meaning: Mus'ab: Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr, governor of Iraq for his brother; his men, bribed by Abd al-Malik, deserted him and he was killed in 71 AH (691 CE).

31.2.4.head: المُختار
31.2.4.meaning: Al-Mukhtar: al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd, who rose in Kufa to avenge al-Husayn; besieged by Mus'ab in the citadel, he went out fighting and was killed.

32.1.4-5.head: اِبن الزُّبَير
32.1.4-5.meaning: Ibn al-Zubayr: Abdallah ibn al-Zubayr, proclaimed caliph in Mecca, who called himself “the one who seeks refuge in the House”; al-Hajjaj besieged and killed him in 72 or 73 AH (692 CE).

32.2.3-4.head: البَيت وَالحَجَر
32.2.3-4.meaning: The House and the Stone: the Kaaba and the Black Stone.

33.1.3-4.head: أَبو الذِّبّان
33.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Dhubban: “father of flies”, Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, the Umayyad caliph, nicknamed for his bad breath, says Ibn Badrun; he died in 86 AH (705 CE).

33.1.5.head: قاضِيَة
33.1.5.meaning: Qadiya: “a deadly one”, from qada ala, to finish off; here his sword. The editions have qadiba, “cutting”, or madiya, “keen”.

33.2.2.head: اللَّطيم
33.2.2.meaning: Al-Latim: “the slapped one”, Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq, called the devil's slapped one for a twist in his mouth; Abd al-Malik killed him with his own hands.

34.1.3.head: زَيد
34.1.3.meaning: Zayd: Zayd ibn Ali, great-grandson of Ali ibn Abi Talib, who rebelled in Kufa against the caliph Hisham and was killed in 122 AH (740 CE).

35.1.2-4.head: الوَليد بن يَزيد
35.1.2-4.meaning: Al-Walid son of Yazid: al-Walid II, the Umayyad caliph, notorious for wine and song, killed by rebels in 126 AH (744 CE); his head was paraded in Damascus.

36.1.1.head: حَبابَة
36.1.1.meaning: Habbaba: the singing girl of the Umayyad caliph Yazid II; he flicked a pomegranate seed or a grape at her as she laughed, and she choked on it and died, says Ibn al-Jawzi.

37.1.4.head: السَّفّاح
37.1.4.meaning: Al-Saffah: Abu al-Abbas Abdallah, the first Abbasid caliph, who came to power in 132 AH (750 CE).

37.2.3.head: مَروان
37.2.3.meaning: Marwan: Marwan II, the last Umayyad caliph in the East, caught and killed at Busir in Egypt in 132 AH (750 CE); his head was sent to al-Saffah.

38.1.3-4.head: الرّوح الأَمين
38.1.3-4.meaning: “The Faithful Spirit”: Gabriel, as the Quran calls him (26:193).

38.2.2.head: فَخّ
38.2.2.meaning: Fakhkh: a place a few miles from Mecca where al-Husayn ibn Ali, a descendant of al-Hasan, and other members of Ali's house were killed in 169 AH (786 CE).

39.1.2.head: جَعفَر
39.1.2.meaning: Ja'far: Ja'far ibn Yahya the Barmakid, Harun al-Rashid's vizier and companion, executed by him in 187 AH (803 CE).

39.1.3.head: الفَضل
39.1.3.meaning: Al-Fadl: al-Fadl ibn Yahya, Ja'far's brother, imprisoned after the fall of the Barmakids.

39.2.1-2.head: الشَّيخ يَحيى
39.2.1-2.meaning: Old Yahya: Yahya ibn Khalid the Barmakid, father of Ja'far and al-Fadl, Harun's vizier, who died in prison.

40.1.3.head: الأَمين
40.1.3.meaning: Al-Amin: Muhammad al-Amin, Harun al-Rashid's heir, killed in the war with his brother al-Ma'mun in 198 AH (813 CE).

40.2.1.head: جَعفَر
40.2.1.meaning: Ja'far: the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil, murdered by Turkish guards on his son al-Muntasir's orders in 247 AH (861 CE).

40.2.3-4.head: الأَعبُد الغُدُر
40.2.3-4.meaning: “The treacherous slaves”: the Turkish slave soldiers of the Abbasid court.

41.1.4.head: المُستَعين
41.1.4.meaning: Al-Musta'in: an Abbasid caliph who abdicated in 252 AH (866 CE) on sworn promises of safety, and was then killed.

41.2.3.head: المُعتَزّ
41.2.3.meaning: Al-Mu'tazz: the Abbasid caliph who succeeded al-Musta'in; the Turks deposed and killed him in 255 AH (869 CE).

42.1.5.head: مُعتَمِد
42.1.5.meaning: Mu'tamid: a title borne by several rulers, among them the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tamid, killed by his nephew, says Ibn Badrun, and al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad of Seville.

42.2.4.head: مُقتَدِر
42.2.4.meaning: Muqtadir: anyone with that title, among them the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir, killed fighting his own general in 320 AH (932 CE), with whose story Ibn Badrun ends his commentary.

43.1.3.head: مَأمون
43.1.3.meaning: Ma'mun: “the one who is safe”, a title borne first by the caliph al-Ma'mun, son of Harun al-Rashid.

43.1.4.head: مُؤتَمَن
43.1.4.meaning: Mu'taman: “the trusted”, the title of Harun al-Rashid's third heir, al-Qasim, who was set aside, and of later princes.

43.2.3.head: مَنصور
43.2.3.meaning: Mansur: “the aided”, the title of the caliph al-Mansur and of al-Mansur ibn Abi Amir in al-Andalus, among others.

43.2.4.head: مُنتَصِر
43.2.4.meaning: Muntasir: “the victor”, the title of the caliph al-Muntasir, who had his father killed and lived only six months after.

44.1.2-3.head: آل عَبّاس
44.1.2-3.meaning: The house of Abbas: the Abbasid caliphs of Baghdad, descendants of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas.

44.1.4.meaning: La'an: said to one who stumbles: get up, be well.

44.2.2.head: زَبّاء
44.2.2.meaning: Zabba': a shaggy she-camel, and so a dire calamity; the proverb has it that every shaggy camel shies, because the wind blows its hair in its eyes.

45.1.1-2.head: بَنو المُظَفَّر
45.1.1-2.meaning: Sons of al-Muzaffar: the Aftasid kings of Badajoz, named after al-Muzaffar Muhammad, father of al-Mutawakkil Umar.

47.2.5.head: الثُّغَر
47.2.5.meaning: Thughar: gaps, the exposed places on a frontier.

48.1.3-4.head: عَوالي الخَطّ
48.1.3-4.meaning: “The heights of al-Khatt”: spears; al-Khatt, on the Gulf coast, was famous for them.

49.1.4.head: البيض
49.1.4.meaning: Bid: “the white ones”, swords; the word is also praise for noble men, “white of face”.

52.2.5.head: عُمَر
52.2.5.meaning: Umar: al-Mutawakkil Umar, the last Aftasid king of Badajoz, killed by the Almoravids with his sons al-Fadl and al-Abbas.

53.1.3-4.head: الفَضل وَالعَبّاس
53.1.3-4.meaning: Al-Fadl and al-Abbas: al-Mutawakkil's sons, put to death with him by the Almoravids.

54.1.4.head: النَّسران
54.1.4.meaning: Al-Nasran: the two Eagles, stars: the Flying Eagle (Altair) and the Falling Eagle (Vega).

59.1.5.head: شَرائِع
59.1.5.meaning: Shara'i': watering places at a river's edge.

61.2.3-4.meaning: Ya lallah: “O God”, a cry for help.

62.2.2-3.head: أَحلام عاد
62.2.2-3.meaning: “The minds of Ad”: a proverb for weighty judgment, after the ancient people of Ad; ahlam is the plural of hilm, mind, and also of hulm, dream.

62.2.6.head: الخَضِر
62.2.6.meaning: Al-Khidr: the mysterious guide of Moses in the Quran, proverbial for his knowledge and said to live for ever. Al-Fath ibn Khaqan's Qala'id al-Iqyan has the same reading; al-Mu'jib has al-Hadr, a ruined city, and Ibn Badrun's text al-khatar, danger.

63.1.1.head: وَيلُمِّه
63.1.1.meaning: Waylummih: “woe to his mother”, an exclamation of awe.

64.1.1-5.meaning: “Who is there for me with them, and there is no one”: a wish cut off by despair.

66.2.6.head: الصَّدَر
66.2.6.meaning: Sadar: coming back from the water, after wird, going down to it.

68.1.5.head: أُخت
68.1.5.meaning: Its sister: la'alla, “it may be”, which the grammarians pair with asa as words of hope.

70.2.1.head: شَقاشِق
70.2.1.meaning: Shaqashiq: the bladders a camel stallion puffs from its mouth as it roars; figuratively, loud eloquence.
